en: All forty were sons of forty khans.
Each had quarreled with his own people
And come to settle in Talas,
Becoming choros to your father, Sultan Manas.
A choro who came without a horse:
For the choro who came without a horse,
With mountain-sheep legs and copper forelegs,
He provided the finest horse to ride.
From the people he had reached,
Your khan father set him apart
And made him known to all.
A choro who came without a coat:
For the choro who came without a coat,
With a golden collar and copper sleeves,
Double mail with links like larks' eyes,
A metal-thread jacket with a broad collar,
Handsome and proof against shots:
He clothed him in the finest coat.
A choro who came without livestock:
Pied-headed horses upon the hills,
Argymaks and swift steeds together,
All exceptional tulpars:
Your royal father, Khan Manas,
Gave each his own allotted share.
For the choro who came without a home,
He chose a white great yurt and settled him inside.
For the choro who came unmarried,
He ascertained his circumstances;
With a thimble mouth and dark eyes,
From among the graceful beauties,
He procured a wife.
Your father's forty choros:
I sent them on holy war against the Chinese;
Into the hands of the forty choros,
I placed forty spears;
I had them wreak a mighty slaughter.
Grasping spears, breaking the ranks,
Those whose hour had come falling to shots,
Drenched in dark blood,
Fighting without retreat:
Your father's forty choros
I pictured in a row.
Before the forty choros,
Their wits utterly scattered:
Of Kakanchyn's Beijing,
I pictured its panic.
Barefoot and bareheaded,
Hurrying and stumbling in confusion,
I pictured their flight.
The spear-bearing Muslims,
Driving in the Chinese:
I pictured them breaking them apart.
Falling this way and that,
The masses of Chinese and Manchu:
I pictured their deaths.
Teeming like ants,
Swarming thicker than mosquitoes:
I pictured the people of Beijing.
'When my orphan returns,
Let him see the tumult,' I thought.
Beijing with its Kakanchy:
I pictured its wonders.
'Let him take it firmly to heart;
His father's deeds,
Let my orphan hold them in mind,' I thought,
And made the picture as a memorial.
When you enter among those pictures,
Your heart will be sorely shaken;
The tears will pour from your eyes.
Your fierce father, Khan Manas,
Will seem to be alive.
Grieving for your father, my only one,
Do not let your heart be turned astray;
Do not suddenly take your own life!
When you enter the mausoleum,
Unless I have spoken falsely,
The mausoleum's interior will resound;
It will murmur and speak.
Many signs will appear;
My foal, your heart will be sorely shaken.
If those signs appear in the mausoleum,
Go to the six villains;
The possessions your father left,
Enter without wavering and bring them back!
If those signs are absent,
Return without going farther;
Say, 'I saw no sign,'
And tell your ill-fated mother.
Such is the matter of the mausoleum.
Let us leave that aside;
Let us begin with what lies nearer.
If I tell my sorrows, they are many.
When you draw back this way,
When you return toward here,
At Zhanyryk's Zhar-Kyya,
Along the winding single path,
When you reach that road:
The ownerless livestock your father left.
Your mother wandered, struggling to survive,
And fled here to Bukhara.
Your father had gone to the other world;
'When the khan is dead, for the old man
Tending livestock will be a solace,' she thought.
The ownerless livestock your father Manas left,
She entrusted for safekeeping
And gave to Khan Bakai.
Those camels he has been tending
Must now have reached seven hundred.
Among those camels,
The father of camels is the gray male;
The mother of camels is the pale she-camel.
They must know you are coming.
Restless when put out to pasture,
Not grazing when let loose,
Those camels along the hills
Must have been yearning for you.
Mature she-camels and young camels
Will come waddling out before you.
Every one of them will bellow,
My ocean, my son Semetey;
When you see those camels,
Your ocean of blood will cry out.
Their humps will sway,
Their long hair will shake;
They will circle round, rumbling,
All calling and bellowing together.
Their long hair will part,
Their tears will pour down;
They will stand sniffing you and bellowing.
They must know you are coming;
My great one, my son, listen:
They must have been yearning for you.
When you see those camels of yours,
Your heart will be sorely shaken.
'When even beasts behave like this,
What of my own soul?' you will say.
My foal, your tears will pour down.
Among those camels,
A dark nar with a broad hump,
With a flapping front lip
And a swaying rear hump:
Zhelmayan, left by your father Manas.
It would bring reproach to return without seeing him.
Zhelmayan's halter—
Bring it with you, my orphan;
This trust is yours alone.
The dark nar with the broad hump
From your leopard father Manas:
Your inheritance that remains.
Let me tell you his mature years;
My foal, my son, listen:
He must have reached ninety-five,
Zhelmayan, this very year.
He must be ninety-five mature years old.
When your lion father died,
He remained in mourning.
For twelve years now,
That Zhelmayan standing there
Has lain down without rising.
Huddled like a quail,
Zhelmayan has sunk upon his knees.
With tears welling in his eyes,
Zhelmayan has let them fall.
When one sees Zhelmayan,
He torments a mortal's soul;
No person can stand looking on.
Zhelmayan, left by your father:
Dust has covered his long hair;
Spots have covered both his eyes.
When Zhelmayan was strong,
Your leopard father Manas
Would load his shot and powder upon him
And campaign far, far away.
Sixty lengths of fine white cloth, shot and powder:
Zhelmayan would carry them loaded.
All manner of equipment,
Your leopard father Manas
Would pack upon Zhelmayan.
Encountered through the unseen world,
For your father blessed by Kyzyr,
He was found after great hardship.
A star streaked through the sky;
With your father Manas the lion,
In the desert of Median,
He was joined by God's favor.
With your father, Prince Manas,
He was united when little as a louse,
He joined him when small as a thumb.
His swiftness was proven to the people;
The inheritance left by your khan father Manas.
The wind cannot match his trot;
No beast can match his walk.
He traveled everywhere,
The four corners of the world:
He visited them in twelve days.
Your blessed father, your protecting spirit,
To the khoja in Kokon,
When his reach extended,
To the petition officer in Bukhara,
When he gave his commands,
When your father, across the earth,
Was working wonders,
Herding white deer and making them cattle,
Throwing the whole world into turmoil,
Driving gray deer and making them cattle,
Throwing every land he saw into confusion,
Across the earth, turmoil,
When he was raising it,
Smashing every place he reached,
When he was taking them over,
For the lightly equipped choros
Zhelmayan carried dispatches.
To the four corners of the world,
When your lordly father was alive,
Zhelmayan carried news.
Gathering the gold in great quantities,
They must have loaded him without stint.
When Zhelmayan would not rise,
Your uncle Bakai must have borne the hardship.
Pulling up feather grass to feed him,
Giving him water from a leather bucket,
He must have died before his death.
Khan Bakai, your father's sworn brother,
Must have suffered terrible humiliation.
Zhelmayan must have lain without rising;
Khan Bakai must have endured torment.
With no tongue to tell his grief,
He must have burned and ached within.
'When Semetey comes, he will sacrifice me
As an offering for Manas,' he must have said,
And prayed to God for it.
'When will my orphan come?'
Zhelmayan, left by Manas,
Must have grieved for twelve years.
When you go to the camels,
Zhelmayan will come trotting;
With tears welling in his eyes,
Zhelmayan will come shedding them.
Circling round you,
Zhelmayan will come walking.
Sniffing once at your right side,
Sniffing once at your left side,
Toward your khan father's great grave,
Dashing toward that great grave,
Zhelmayan will run away.
The dark cliff where your father is buried:
When he reaches that dark cliff,
Laying his head toward the north,
Taking the dark cliff for his pillow,
Zhelmayan will kneel down.
With tears welling in his eyes,
Zhelmayan will let them fall.
Planting his halter firmly on the ground,
Zhelmayan will crouch down.
Without rising when whipped,
Zhelmayan will sink to his knees.
